findings.claim: Every new Swift guard this round is a `body.includes(...)` / occurrence-count string pin, which detects EDITS to the quoted lines but is structurally blind to an INSERTED line. Appending `; if 1 == 1 { return false }` to Daily.swift:455 (objViolated) or Game.swift:683 (autoSendWouldBreakTier) leaves every pin satisfied while disabling every iOS tier ✗ chip and both iOS auto-play refusals — i.e. shipping bug/WF-4 back verbatim on iOS with a green suite.
findings.note: MUTATION-PROVEN this round: x-ios-objViolated-early-false SURVIVED, x-ios-autoSend-early-false SURVIVED (my manifest, 0 errors, so the survivals are real applies). Cheap insertion-proof fix without a Swift test target: for these two functions assert the NORMALISED WHOLE BODY equals an expected string (assert.equal, not includes) rather than asserting each snippet is present; or at minimum pin the head exactly, e.g. `func objViolated(_ obj: Objective, _ t: Attempt) -> Bool { let p = obj.param switch obj.id {` and `guard let ch = liveChallenge else { return false } var t = liveAttempt() let silverWasLive =`, so nothing can be spliced in front of the switch. The implementer's honest 'Swift has no test target' note explains the limit but does not remove it — the pin can be made insertion-proof for the same cost.

findings.claim: The new behavioural guard on the shipped autoSendWouldBreakTier only exercises day 29, whose Gold is a split-at objective — it reads neither `moves` nor `moveIdx` of the projected attempt. So the look-ahead's projection depth is unconstrained: changing index.html:700 `moves:moveCount+1` to `moves:moveCount` survives the whole suite, and so does replacing index.html:701 `moveIdx:moveCount+1` with a constant. Concrete failure: on a day whose Silver/Gold is the 'moves' family with budget N, at moveCount == N the projected attempt reports N instead of N+1, objViolated returns false, and auto-play spends the budget-breaking move with zero player input — the exact bug/WF-4 shape, on a family the new tests never touch. `moveIdx` is what rank-rush and suit-sprint deadlines are read from, same story.
findings.note: MUTATION-PROVEN: my mutants x-web-lookahead-depth-off (moves:moveCount+1 -> moves:moveCount) and x-web-lookahead-moveidx-off (moveIdx:moveCount+1 -> moveIdx:1) both SURVIVED the full suite (manifest ran with 0 errors). The whole objViolated table in web-behaviour.test.mjs does not help here — it calls objViolated directly with hand-built attempts, so it never sees which attempt autoSendWouldBreakTier builds. Cheapest fix: a direct unit case on web.autoSendWouldBreakTier with a synthetic 'moves' challenge at the exact budget boundary (moveCount == N must refuse, moveCount == N-2 must allow), and one rank-rush case that depends on moveIdx.

findings.claim: extractDecl's regex is `^[ \t]*(function|const|let)[ \t]+NAME\b`, so it matches an INDENTED (nested) declaration anywhere in index.html, not the top-level one the docstring promises, and the first textual match wins. A future local helper with a colliding name silently swaps the code under test with no error, breaking the load-bearing 'we run the shipped code' property of the whole round.
findings.note: CONFIRMED by experiment on a scratch copy of index.html: injecting `  const objViolated = () => false;` at line 100 (1578 lines above the real one at 1678) made loadWeb() succeed and return the decoy — web.objViolated({id:'moves',param:{N:1}}, {moves:99}) came back false, no throw. No live defect today: I checked all 29 NAMES and each has exactly one declaration, at column 0. The exposure is that several lifted names are exported but never called by any assertion (isSafeAutoplay, autoFinishWouldWin, evaluate, gradeOf, labelOf, makeObjective, foldHome), so a shadow on those would not be caught by a failing test either. One-character fix: drop `[ \t]*` from the regex.
